Mahbubey Alam with Mafuza Begum, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Md Fazlul Karim with ABM Mahbub, Advocates ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Nurul Haque (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Anowara Begum and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule are that, one Mossammat Anowara Begum instituted the Other Suit No.18 of 1980 on 5-2-1980 in the Court of the Munsif, Thakurgaon, Dinajpur praying for setting aside the ex parte decree passed on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No. 100 of 1978 declaring the same illegal. collusive and not binding upon her and the learned Munsif by his judgment and decree dated 30-1-1982 has been pleased to decree the suit on contest with costs declaring the ex parte decree obtained by the defendant No.1, namely, Nurul Haque, on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 is not binding upon the plaintiff. 

 3. As against the said judgment and decree the defendants preferred the Other Appeal No.24 of 1992 and on 14-6-1984 the appeal was allowed by the learned appellate Court, by its Judgment and decree, setting aside the Judgment and decree of the learned trial Court and remanding the suit back to the trial Court with direction to the Learned Munsif to give an opportunity to the plaintiff to amend her plaint. On 25-2-1985 the case record was received by the trial Court from the appellate Court back on remand and the learned trial Court returned the plaint to the plaintiff for filling it before an appropriate Court and the 'plaintiff has re-filed it by amending the plaint in the Court of the Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon and the suit has been registered as the Other Suit No.5 of 1984 and during trial of the case neither party adduced any additional evidence, but relied upon the evidence recorded earlier in the Other Class Suit No.18 of 1980. 

 4. On conclusion of the trial the learned Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon has been pleased to dismiss the suit by his judgment and decree dated 28-5-1992 and being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff has preferred the Title Appeal No.19 of 1992 and by judgment and decree dated 27-5-1993 the learned Additional District Judge. Thakurgaon, has been pleased to allow the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the learned trial Court and declaring the ex parte decree passed in the Other Class Suit No.1 00 of 1978 on 24-5-1979. by the learned Assistant Judge, Thakurgaon illegal, void, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff- appellant also declaring the title of the plaintiff in the suit property directing the defendant No.1 to vacate the suit land by demolishing and removing structures and declaring also khas possession of the plaintiff in the suit land on eviction of the defendant No.1 as aforesaid. 

 5. As against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon in Title (Other) Appeal No.19 of 1992 the defendant-respondent has preferred this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule together with an order of stay of all further proceedings of the Title Execution Case No.5 of 1993 pending in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Thakurgaon. 

 6. Facts as appears from the pleadings of the parties and the judgments of the Courts below are that in the Other Class Suit No.18 of 1980 the plaintiff Mossammat Anowara Begum stated that the suit land originally belonged to one Subarna Probha Biswas and the CS Khatian No.420 was finally published in her name. Subsequently, the suit property was put to auction in the Certificate Case No.15311958-59 and she along with the defendant No.3 namely, Hanuman Das Agarwala purchased the entire land of the suit Khatian on auction held on 9-11-1959, with equal shares. The sale was confirmed on 9-1-1960 and they got delivery of possession of the suit land from the Court on 16-2-1960 and thus they acquired the right, title interests and possession of the suit land extinguishing the interests of Subarna Probha Biswas. 

 The defendant No.3 Hanuman Das Agarwala sold his half share to one Upendra Nath Barman who subsequently, filed a Partition Suit in the Court of Munsif: Thakurgaon, Dinajpur being No.143 of 1960 against the plaintiff and her husband and the suit was dismissed on contest. An appeal was preferred being Partition Appeal No.68 of 1961 and the learned Subordinate Judge. Dinajpur was also pleased to dismiss the appeal on contest. 

 Thereafter, Upendra Nath Barman again filed the Title Suit No.4 of 1963 in the same Court and obtained an ex parte decree on 2-9-1963. The present plaintiff, Mossammat Anowara Begum has then filed a suit for cancellation of that ex parte decree being the Other Suit No.37 of 1966 in the same Court and the said ex parte decree has been set aside and the original suit was restored to its original file and number and Upendra Nath ultimately, obtained a decree in that Title Suit. 

 The defendant No.1 has obtained an ex parte decree from the Court of the Munsif, Thakurgaon, in the Other Class Suit No. 100 of 1978 after he was defeated in the VP Miscellaneous Caseie after release of the suit property and got the ex parte decree behind the knowledge of the plaintiff, in respect of 19 decimal of land on 24-5-1979. The plaintiff was not made a party in that suit intentionally and her title has been clouded by that ex parte decree and thus, she has been obliged to institute the instant suit. 

 11. During the re-trial of the suit on remand, learned Munsif has framed two issues, namely, whether the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and barred by limitation for the learned appellate Court has directed to decide those two points in its order of remand and the learned trial Court held that the plaintiff has proved her title in the entire land but the defendant No.1, Nurul Haque is in possession of 19 sataks of land and the plaintiff failed to prove that the defendant No.1 entered into the suit land' as tenant of the plaintiff. She did not produce any deed of tenancy agreement or rent receipts in this respect and her witnesses are partisan and their evidence are not reliable to the effect that the defendant No.1 entered into the suit land as tenant of the plaintiff. 

 12. On perusal of the document namely, the tax paying receipt of the Municipality of the year 1965, produced by the defendant No.1, the learned trial Court held that the defendant No.1 is in possession of that 19 sataks of land from 15/16 years ago. In accordance with the auction purchase dated 12-12- 1960. the plaintiff got possession in the southern portion or the suit plot and she could not explain as to how she got possession in 28'/2 steaks of land in the northern portion of the plot. By auction. Hanuman Das Agarwala got possession of this plot which he sold out to Upendra Nath Barman by a registered deed. Upendra Nath Barman instituted the Partition Suit praying for separate shaham where he lost upto appeal and, on the contrary, he won the Title Suit upto the appellate Court and in that Partition Suit this defendant No.1 was also a defendant. From that period this defendant is an illegal occupier in the suit land and his possession is adverse to all and continuous. The plaintiff has purchased from Upendra Nath Barman on 8-8-1970 by a registered deed measuring an area of 28-1/2 sataks in the northern portion of the plot but she could not prove acquiring her possession under the Kabala. The plaintiff also could not prove whether her vendor Upendra Nath Barman executed the decree which he obtained in his Partition Suit. The title of the plaintiff in the suit land is mere paper title and that she inserted her claim for recovery of possession on 29-9-1984 by way of amendment of the plaint. It could not be said that the possession of the defendant No.1 was not adverse to the plaintiff only because he took lease of it from the Government as Enemy Property. The defendant No.1 has enjoyed adverse possession and right, title thereof from 1963 to 1984. Though the ex parte decree was passed on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 without making the plaintiff a party and in her absence, but still it can be said that the decree was passed on finding his possession. The plaintiff has lost her cause of action by not suing from 8-8-1970. to 29-9-1984 and the suit is barred by section 144 of the Limitation Act. But the suit is maintainable in its nature and form. The suit is not hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

 14. The findings of the Learned Appellate Court in the Other Appeal No. 19 of 1992, on the contrary, are that as soon as the defendant No.1 took lease of 7 decimal of land from the Government as Enemy Property, his claim of adverse possession stood relinquished and, as such, the limitation of more than 12 years has been completed. The findings of the learned trial Court on the point of limitation was erroneous. The defendant No. 1 has not acquired any title by adverse possession and he is liable to eviction. The defendant No.1 claimed that he is dwelling in an area of 0.07 sataks of land having his dwelling house and possessing another 12 sataks of contiguous land by growing vegetables and plantation which is a new claim, not raised in the Other Suit No. 100 of 1978. 

 15. Mr Mahbubey Alam appearing with Mrs Mafuza Begum, the learned Advocates, for the petitioner, has advanced mainly threefold arguments: namely, (a) the plaintiff by adducing oral and documentary evidence could not prove the date of her alleged dispossession from the suit land. Relying upon the cases of Jogendra Nath alias Govinda Sarker vs Amulya Chandra Sarker and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 147. Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 100, the learned Advocate submits that since the plaintiff failed to prove induction of the defendant No.1 as her tenant in the suit land, he will be treated under the law, as a hostile possessor and his possession is adverse possession under the law; (b) With reference to the cases of Radhamoni Debi vs Collector and others reported in 27 Indian Appeals 136, Secretary of State vs Debendra Lal, reported in 1934 (Privy Council) 23; Ejas Ali Qidwai and others vs Special Manager. Court of Wards. Balrampur Estate and others reported in 1935 (Privy Council) 53 and Musa Ali vs Nur Ahmed and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 154 the Learned Advocate submits that since the possession of the defendant No.1 was open, overt, continuous and competitive against his competitor, the same has conferred a good title against all except the real owner and since the defendant No.1 has proved by evidence that he is in possession of the suit land the onus of proof was shifted upon the plaintiff to prove that he was inducted by her as her tenant or was her permissive possessor or licensee and in the absence of such proof: the possession of the defendant No.1 is clearly an adverse possession and (c) the defendant No.1 is in possession of the suit land from 1963 without break as it was found by the Courts below and so he has acquired his title in the suit land by way of adverse possession and the Learned appellate Court has erred in law in not holding title in the suit land by adverse possession and the findings and conclusion of the learned appellate Court is liable to be set aside. 

 16. Mr Md Fazlul Karim with Mr ABM Mahbub, the learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party, submits on the other hand, that the suit property was declared Enemy Property in the year 1969 and it remained as such till its release in favour of the plaintiff in the year 1978 and the defendant No.1 got lease of 7 sataks of land from the Government acknowledging and admitting the property to be the property of the Government and thus this period running from 1969-78 could not be added to or deemed to be hostile or adverse possession against the plaintiff. The learned Courts below found that the defendant No.1 has entered into an unlawful possession in 1963 and since the property was declared Enemy Property in 1969 his possession was of only 6 years prior to declaration of Enemy Property. The suit was instituted in 1980 and; as such, the period of his possession is not more than 8 years in all and, as such, he has acquired no adverse possession or title in the suit land. The plaintiff need not prove her constructive possession, since the possession of the defendant No.1 was broken. The defendant No.1 cannot claim his adverse possession in the suit land as was held by their Lordships in the case of Kumar Basanta Roy and others vs Secretary of Stale for India in Council and others reported in 44 Indian Appeals 104. 

 19. It has been variously described eg, (a) abnormal enjoyment. against all the world, but wrongly against the true owner (b) continuous possession against the title of the true owner if continued for the statutory period of limitation except making re-entry or bringing an action (c) Continuous exercise of right or title against the true owner which cannot afterwards be refused, either by re-entry or subsequent acknowledgment (Pannamma Velly vs Achu Thana Union. ILR 1966, 1 Kerala 689). Possession by continuous assertion against the title of the dispossessed owner and actual exclusive possession of the property commenced and continued to a clear right either openly or by a void claim' against a constructive claim adverse against the competitor and actual in continuity, in publicity and to the extent to show that its possession is adverse to the competitor. 

 23. In the instant case, admittedly the property belonged to one Subarna Probha and according to the plaintiff, the property was auction sold and she, together with one Hanuman Das Agarwala (defendant No.3) purchased that property in the auction proceeding and got possession thereof through the Court and subsequently, Hanuman Das sold out his share to one Upendra Nath who instituted a suit praying for his separate saham and he lost the suit upto appeal. He then instituted a Title Suit and obtaining a decree and won up to appeal. The plaintiff purchased the share of Upendra Nath, after being lost in that Title Suit and appeal, by her kabala and became owner of the entire property, in question. The case of the defendant No.1 is that the story of Certificate Case and Auction Sale of the suit property and purchase of the plaintiff are all false. Subarna Probha was the owner and possessor of the suit property and in the Khatian Hanuman Das was recorded as forceful possessor. When Subarna Probha left for' India sometime around the partition of the subcontinent, he got his possession in the property by making a house in the portion where Hanuman Das was the forceful possessor. Subarna Probha's property became Enemy Property and was listed as such in the year 1969 and he got lease of .07 sataks of land from the Government in whom the property was vested and in this area of land he has his homestead and the lease continued till its release in 1978. 

 The learned appellate Court found that the plaintiff's persuasion and chase to the equal share holder of Certificate purchase, Hanuman Das, has finally led to the point of her purchase from Upendra Nath. Upon purchase of the property in auction, the plaintiff got possession in the southern half and Hanuman Das in the northern half of the suit plot. While the plaintiff was trying to come to the northern half of the land in question by way of litigations with Hanuman Das he made an exit by way of transfer to Upendra Nath and Upendra Nath was in possession of this portion. From Upendra Nath the plaintiff has finally purchased it and Upendra Nath had his right, title and possession therein. 

 The learned first trial Court also found possession of the defendant No.1, but since the defendant No.1 could not explain his possession, the Learned Court held that it will not amount as hostile to the plaintiff. In the opinion of the learned remand Court, since before her purchase from Upendra Nath., the defendant No.1 was possessing the half share of Hanuman Das, so his possession was prior to the purchase of the plaintiff. It is hostile against Hanuman Das and also against the plaintiff. Though the plaintiff acquired title, but she did not get the possession of it. 

 In arriving at the aforesaid findings the Learned Courts below committed a grave omission in not looking into the fact, why Upendra Nath lost his Partition Suit upto its appeal against the present plaintiff and why he was compelled to institute a Title Suit instead: especially, why his prayer for separate saham was refused. 

 Send down the lower Court's Record at once.
